engine: offline/engine.js — RC port of src/thermal/rc_model.py (parity-verified), AI surrogate from src/ai_model.py

materials.name: brick
materials.source: ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals 2021 Ch.26 (common brick, ~119 lb/ft3); absorptance/emissivity: ASHRAE 2021 Ch.26 Table 24 (red brick, aged)

materials.name: concrete
materials.source: ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals 2021 Ch.26 (dense concrete ~144 lb/ft3); emissivity: ASHRAE Ch.26 (concrete 0.85-0.95)

materials.name: rcc_slab
materials.source: same dense-concrete row; reinforced concrete approx. as dense concrete (ASHRAE HOF 2021 Ch.26)

materials.name: stone
materials.source: ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals 2021 Ch.26 (granite k ~2.7-3.5 W/mK, 165 lb/ft3)

materials.name: rammed_earth
materials.source: Rammed earth: k 0.6-1.0 W/mK, rho ~1700-2000 kg/m3 (e.g. Hall & Allinson 2009; CIBSE Guide A); absorptance: earth 0.6
materials.notes: verify with local soil test for final submission

materials.name: timber
materials.source: ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals 2021 Ch.26 (yellow pine); cp ~1.63 kJ/kgK

materials.name: mineral_wool
materials.source: ISO 10456 / EN 13162 typical: k 0.035-0.045 W/mK, rho 25-200 kg/m3; absorptance typical for insulation behind cladding

materials.name: eps
materials.source: ISO 10456 / EN 13163 typical: EPS k 0.030-0.040 W/mK, rho 15-30 kg/m3; cp ~1.2-1.5 kJ/kgK (manufacturer datasheets)

materials.name: xps
materials.source: ISO 10456 / EN 13164 typical: XPS k 0.029-0.036 W/mK; cp ~1.4-1.5 kJ/kgK

materials.name: puf_sandwich_panel
materials.source: PUR/PIR panel cores k 0.022-0.028 W/mK (EN 14509, manufacturer datasheets); outer steel skin absorptance 0.5 typical (galvanised, painted)

materials.name: gi_sheet
materials.source: ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals 2021 Ch.26 (steel k ~45-50 W/mK, 490 lb/ft3, cp 0.12 Btu/lbF = 502 J/kgK); galvanised steel solar absorptance 0.5-0.65, emissivity 0.28 (ASHRAE Ch.26 Table 24)

materials.name: mud_brick
materials.source: ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals 2021 Ch.26 (adobe k ~0.57 W/mK, rho ~1900 kg/m3, cp 0.2 Btu/lbF); Chandel & Aggarwal (2017) review of Himalayan vernacular (mud brick k 0.4-0.8 W/mK); absorptance earth 0.6-0.7

materials.name: aerated_concrete
materials.source: ASHRAE Handbook-Fundamentals 2021 Ch.26 (aerated/lightweight concrete k ~0.08-0.25 W/mK, rho 400-800 kg/m3); emissivity 0.9 (ASHRAE Ch.26 Table 24)

materials.name: sheep_wool
materials.source: ISO 10456 / EN 13171 typical sheep-wool insulation k 0.038-0.045 W/mK, rho 15-30 kg/m3 (manufacturer datasheets, e.g. Thermafleece); cp ~1.03 kJ/kgK (Kersten 1949 soil/hygroscopic data)

metrics.note: Test MAE/R2 on a random 20% holdout; per-site MAE from leave-one-site-out training on the other 11 cities.

metadata.name: rc-surrogate-v2
metadata.disclaimer: Estimates from a surrogate trained on the sourced RC engine; the engine remains the source of truth.

designs.name: Composite Brick Studio
designs.tagline: Balanced all-rounder for composite plains climates
designs.rationale: 230 mm brick mass buffers the day-night swing; 50 mm EPS on walls and roof cuts peak solar loads; moderate south glazing admits winter sun without overheating. A sane default for Prayagraj-class composite climates.

designs.name: Desert Thermal-Mass Cell
designs.tagline: Heavy rammed earth for hot-dry amplitude control
designs.rationale: 450 mm rammed earth gives a long thermal lag — peak heat arrives indoors at night when it can be vented. Small north opening with low SHGC limits direct gain; mass does the cooling work in hot-dry deserts.

designs.name: Coastal Light Envelope
designs.tagline: Insulated panel shell for warm-humid coasts
designs.rationale: In warm-humid climates mass stores heat rather than shaving it — the insulated panel shell sheds solar gain fast, a low-SHGC window and shaded orientation limit radiant load, and the envelope stays light for night-time ventilation.

designs.name: Ladakh Vernacular (Stone + Mud Roof)
designs.rationale: The traditional Ladakhi wall recipe — thick stone mass with a flat mud roof — couples huge thermal storage with slow night-time release. The single south window harvests the intense high-altitude winter sun. Included so vernacular practice can be compared against engineered upgrades on the same engine, same weather.

designs.name: Ladakh High-Performance Upgrade
designs.tagline: Sheep-wool + low-e glazing: engineered for -25 °C nights
designs.rationale: 150 mm local sheep-wool insulation on the inside of heavy rammed earth keeps the mass inside the heated volume; the PUF panel roof stops the biggest single loss path; south-facing low-e double glazing admits maximum solar gain (SHGC 0.85) while U 1.6 limits night losses. Designed for Leh/Kargil/Dras winters.

designs.name: Kashmir Valley House
designs.tagline: Brick + wool batt + double glazing for the valley cold
designs.rationale: Kashmir winters are cold but less extreme than Ladakh's: a 345 mm brick wall with 100 mm mineral wool, timber roof deck and clear double glazing balances cost and comfort for valley towns.

designs.name: Rapid Relief Kit
designs.rationale: A factory-made insulated panel box: the core is already the insulation (k ~0.023 W/mK), so it is fast to erect and performs without site-built layers. Small window keeps it robust in transit and on site.

designs.name: Rural Low-Cost Unit
designs.tagline: Mud brick + timber roof at minimal material cost
designs.rationale: Local mud brick and timber framing keep cost and embodied energy low while providing useful thermal mass; honest about its limits (single glazing, no insulation) — the engine quantifies the trade-off.

designs.name: Temperate Comfort Box
designs.tagline: Light-touch envelope for mild upland climates
designs.rationale: Mild climates reward a modest envelope: standard brick, thin insulation and a normal window — enough to damp extremes without paying for heavy cold-climate measures.

designs.name: AAC Insulated High-Altitude Unit
designs.tagline: Aerated concrete + XPS for fast cold-climate build
designs.rationale: AAC blocks (k ~0.18 W/mK) build fast and insulate better than solid masonry; 100 mm XPS takes the envelope into cold-climate territory; low-e double glazing south-facing captures high-altitude sun.

designs.name: Cool-Roof Composite Studio
designs.tagline: Low-conductivity walls + roof insulation for hot plains
designs.rationale: Roof gains dominate the composite-plains heat load, so 75 mm EPS sits above the ceiling slab while the 250 mm aerated-concrete walls carry their own low conductivity. A smaller south window with SHGC 0.5 keeps winter solar gain while trimming summer peaks.

designs.name: Monsoon Hybrid Studio
designs.tagline: Brick mass below, insulated panel roof — dry-in fast
designs.rationale: A wet-season build that closes in quickly: PUF panel roof over brick mass walls, with XPS on the walls to limit conduction. Higher sill keeps the opening above typical local floor-flood levels while preserving light.

designs.name: Cyclone-Resilient Coastal Shell
designs.tagline: Reinforced concrete + XPS against storm coasts
designs.rationale: Low silhouette with a small, high, storm-shuttered opening and a light GI roof that a real build ties down to a reinforced ring beam. The heavy RCC-plus-XPS walls and 5 ACH night ventilation shed humid-day heat without relying on glass.

designs.name: Breezeway Panel Studio
designs.tagline: Light insulated shell that cools by night air
designs.rationale: For humid coasts the night sky is the heat sink: the shell stays light so it sheds daytime gains fast, operable openings give 8 ACH cross-ventilation, and low-SHGC glass plus a reflective metal roof keep daytime solar gain down.

designs.name: Passive-Solar Sunspace Studio
designs.tagline: Big south glass with thermal mass for mild winters
designs.rationale: Temperate winters are mild but real: 2.7 m² of south glass admits low-angle winter sun onto the exposed concrete floor slab, which stores it for the night. EPS on walls and a 150 mm timber roof cut the envelope losses, and the overhang geometry suits upland sun angles.

designs.name: Desert Night-Purge Cell
designs.tagline: Rammed earth lag plus deliberate night ventilation
designs.rationale: Where nights drop 15 K below days, mass alone works only if the stored heat can leave: this cell couples 350 mm rammed-earth walls with 6 ACH purge openings for after-sunset ventilation and XPS under the roof slab to kill the daytime top gain.

designs.name: Super-Insulated Cold Cell
designs.tagline: 150 mm XPS + solar glass for deep-winter plateaus
designs.rationale: For -25 °C plateau nights the envelope is everything: 150 mm XPS continuous insulation, low-conductivity AAC walls, and the best glazing in the catalogue (U 1.1) kept on the south side with SHGC 0.62 so the winter sun still pays in.

designs.name: Insulated Rapid-Relief Cell
designs.tagline: Deployable panel shelter with winter-rated insulation
designs.rationale: The relief kit's sibling for cold nights and hot afternoons alike: the same fast flat-pack panel envelope, plus 50 mm mineral-wool liner where the plain kit has none — one deployable design, wider climate reach.

results.engine: src/thermal/rc_model.simulate (design weeks on real hourly weather)
